And I'm Conor. Today's episode is all about Programming with Scratch, which for a lot of you will be your very first programming language.

We'll cover the Scratch window, events and sequence, coordinates, costumes and animation, loops, decisions, variables, messages between sprites, making your own blocks, simulations, debugging, and finally how to plan, build and test a game.
That's a lot, so let's get going.
Scratch is a free programming language made by the Lifelong Kindergarten group at the MIT Media Lab in America. It first came out in two thousand and seven.
Instead of typing code, you drag coloured blocks and snap them together, a bit like Lego. So no spelling mistakes and no missing semicolons.
But don't be fooled into thinking it's babyish. The ideas you learn in Scratch, like sequence, selection, loops and variables, are exactly the same ideas you'll use in C sharp later on.
Let's do a quick tour of the screen. Top right is the stage. That's where your project actually runs. Think of it as the cinema screen.
The characters on the stage are called sprites. The Scratch Cat is the famous one. And the picture behind everything on the stage is called a backdrop.
On the left is the blocks palette, the box of Lego, sorted into colour-coded categories: Motion, Looks, Sound, Events, Control, Sensing, Operators, Variables and My Blocks.
And in the middle is the scripts area, your workbench, where you join blocks into scripts. A script is just a stack of blocks that runs from top to bottom.
One thing that catches people out. Every sprite has its own scripts. If your cat won't move, check you didn't build the script on the wrong sprite.
Next up: events and sequence. A script doesn't do anything until something starts it. That something is an event.
Like clicking the green flag, pressing a key, clicking on a sprite, or receiving a message. The yellow event blocks are called hat blocks, because they sit on top of a script like a hat.
Then the blocks underneath run in sequence. One after another, from the top down. Change the order and you change what happens.
Pause and test yourself. Ryan's sprite should walk across the stage and then say I made it. But his say block is above his move block. What goes wrong?
It says I made it before it's moved anywhere. Swap the two blocks round and the sequence is fixed.
Also remember computers are fast. Four move blocks in a row with no waits looks like one big jump. Add a wait if you want to see each step.
Now coordinates. The stage is a grid, just like in maths. It's four hundred and eighty steps wide and three hundred and sixty steps tall.
x goes from minus two hundred and forty on the left to two hundred and forty on the right. y goes from minus one hundred and eighty at the bottom to one hundred and eighty at the top.
And the very centre is nought, nought. You always write x first, then y. Along the corridor, then up the stairs.
There are two kinds of motion block. Go to x y, and set x to, send a sprite to an exact spot. Change x by, change y by, and move steps, move it from wherever it is now.
Pause and test yourself. A sprite is at forty, minus thirty. It does change x by sixty, then change y by fifty. Where is it?
x is forty add sixty, which is one hundred. y is minus thirty add fifty, which is twenty. So it's at one hundred, twenty.
And the classic bug: using set x to ten when you meant change x by ten. Set puts the sprite at the same spot every time, so it never moves along.
Directions are worth knowing too. Ninety is right, nought is up, one hundred and eighty is down and minus ninety is left.
Next, looks and sound. A costume is one picture a sprite can show. The Scratch Cat has two: legs together and legs apart.
Switch between them quickly with next costume, inside a loop, and the cat looks like it's walking. That's animation. It's how a flip book works, and how cartoons work too.
But put a short wait in, about nought point two seconds. No wait and it's a blur. A two second wait and it's very jerky.
For sounds, start sound plays the sound and carries straight on. Play sound until done waits for the sound to finish first.
Right, loops. Repeating blocks is called iteration. Drawing a square without a loop takes eight blocks: move, turn, move, turn, and so on.
With a loop it's repeat four, with move a hundred steps and turn ninety degrees inside. Three blocks. Shorter, easier to read and easier to change.
There are three loops in Scratch. Repeat ten is a count-controlled loop: it runs a set number of times.
Repeat until is a condition-controlled loop. It keeps going until its condition becomes true, like repeat until touching edge.
And forever is an infinite loop. It only stops when you click the red stop sign. That's why nothing can go underneath it.
Here's a handy rule for shapes. The turn is three hundred and sixty divided by the number of sides. So a hexagon, six sides, is a sixty degree turn.
Pause and test yourself. What turn do you need for a regular pentagon, five sides?
Three hundred and sixty divided by five is seventy-two degrees. Repeat five, move, turn seventy-two.
One more loop bug. If you put next costume under the loop instead of inside it, it only runs once, after the loop finishes.
Now decisions. Choosing which blocks to run is called selection. If then has one path. If then else has two: one for true and one for false.
The gap in an if block is pointy at the ends, and only true or false blocks fit there. Those are called Boolean blocks.
Sensing blocks give you lots of those. Touching apple, key space pressed, touching the colour black. And ask and wait lets the user type an answer, which is stored in the answer block.
Here's the big mistake. An if block checks once, at the moment it runs. So if you want a game to notice when you touch the lava, put the if inside a forever loop so it keeps checking.
Fun fact: Scratch's equals block ignores capital letters. Belfast, all lower case, counts as equal to Belfast with a capital B. C sharp is much fussier.
On to variables. A variable is a named store that holds a value that can change. Score, lives, time.
Set score to nought puts in an exact value. Change score by one adds to it. And change lives by minus one takes a life away.
Always set your variables at the start of the green flag script. Otherwise your new game starts with last game's score.

Variables hold different data types. Integers are whole numbers, like three lives. Floats have a decimal point, like two point five. Strings are text, like a player's name. And Booleans are just true or false.
Scratch works the data type out for you, but C sharp makes you choose, so it's good to know them now.

Then there are the green operator blocks. Add, subtract, multiply and divide. Less than, equals and greater than. Join for text. And pick random one to six, which gives a whole number from one to six, including both ends. Perfect for a dice.
Pause and test yourself. Score starts at nought. Change by five, change by five, then set score to score times two. What's the score?
Five, then ten, then ten times two is twenty.
Next: broadcasts. In a game, lots of sprites need to work together. When you click Start, the title disappears, the music starts and the apples begin to fall.
So the Start button sends a broadcast, a message that goes to every sprite and the stage. Any script that begins with when I receive start then runs.
It's like the school intercom. One announcement, and each class decides what to do about it.
And the names must match exactly. If one sprite sends game over with a space, and another is waiting for gameover with no space, nothing happens. Pick from the drop-down to be safe.
Now one of my favourites: My Blocks. In the pink My Blocks category you can make your own custom block.
You give it a name, like jump, and put the blocks it should run under a define hat block. Then your main script just says jump.
This is abstraction: hiding the detail you don't need and giving it a simple name. Like saying make toast, instead of listing every step of using a toaster.
And you can add inputs. A block called draw shape, with inputs for sides and size, can draw a hexagon, a square or a triangle, all from one definition.
In C sharp, a custom block is called a function, and its inputs are called parameters. So you're already learning GCSE ideas.
Then simulations. A model is a simplified version of a real system. A simulation runs the model to see what happens.

Our first one is a bouncing ball. A gravity variable makes the speed change every moment, so the ball falls faster and faster. And each bounce keeps only eighty percent of the speed, so the bounces get lower.
Change gravity to something small and it floats down like it's on the Moon. That's the key idea: change a variable and you change the outcome.
The second one is rabbits on an island. Twenty rabbits, growing by fifty percent a year. After one year, thirty. Then forty-five. Then about sixty-eight. Then about a hundred and one.
But remember models leave things out. Real rabbits run out of food and space. So always ask: what has my model left out?
Now debugging. A bug is a mistake in a program, and debugging is finding and fixing it.
Because blocks only fit together properly, Scratch almost never has syntax errors. Instead you get logic errors. The program runs, but it does the wrong thing.
The best tool is tracing. Step through the script one block at a time, writing down what happens to each variable, just like the computer would.
Here's a sneaky one. A game ends when score equals ten, but each apple is worth three points. Score goes nine, then twelve. It's never exactly ten, so the game never ends.
The fix is to check score greater than nine instead. And when debugging, change one thing at a time, then test again.
Last section: making a game. Programmers work in cycles: plan, develop, test, refine, and then round again. That's iterative development.
Planning starts with who the game is for. A game for a five-year-old needs big pictures and easy controls. A game for your form class can be faster.
You can sum that up in a user story. As a, I want, so that. For example: As a Year 8 pupil with five minutes at break, I want a quick game with a score, so that I can try to beat my friends.
Our example is Orchard Catch. Armagh's the Orchard County, so apples fall from the top and you catch them in a basket with the arrow keys. Three lives, thirty seconds.
Build one feature at a time, and test each one with a test table: the test, the expected result, the actual result, and pass or fail.
Use three kinds of test data. Normal, like catching an apple. Boundary, like losing your very last life. And erroneous, like pressing a key the game doesn't use.
Then refine. Fix the bugs, watch real users play, improve it, and go round the cycle again. And after any fix, retest everything, not just the bit that broke.
Let's recap. Scratch scripts are started by events and run in sequence, top to bottom.
The stage goes from minus two forty to two forty across, and minus one eighty to one eighty up and down, with nought, nought in the middle.
Loops give you iteration: repeat, repeat until and forever. If and if else give you selection, and put your ifs inside a forever loop.
Variables store values like score and lives, as integers, floats, strings or Booleans. Reset them at the start of every game.
Broadcasts let sprites talk to each other, and My Blocks are abstraction, a first step towards functions and parameters.
And develop in cycles: plan for a real user, develop, test with a test table, and refine.
That's Programming with Scratch. Now go and try the quiz on each page, and then open Scratch and make something brilliant.
Thanks for listening. See you next time.
